extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and readers/practitioners of poetry and drama (Elizabethan-era literary practitioners)
extracted.subtask_short: writing and judging poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and critiquing poetry and stage drama: what makes poetry virtuous, memorable, and fit for performance; how plays should observe unity, decorum, and proper structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should teach and move to virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: No learning is so good as that which teacheth and moveth to virtue, and none can both teach and move thereto so much as poesy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poem/play both instructs (teaches moral truth) and moves emotion toward virtuous action; examples cited include Æneas as a model of self-governance, piety, and courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical poetry as highest kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroical ... is not only a kind, but the best and most accomplished kind, of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether heroic/epic treatment presents lofty images of worthies that 'inflameth the mind with desire to be worthy' and supplies counsel on how to be worthy (uses exemplary figures across situations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet creates matter (maker, not borrower)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet only bringeth his own stuff, and doth not learn a conceit out of a matter, but maketh matter for a conceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess originality and generative imagination: the poet is expected to produce material and conceits rather than merely transcribe existing subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse/rhythm aids memory and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse far exceedeth prose in the knitting up of the memory ... those words which are fittest for memory, are likewise most convenient for knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms that enhance retention and teaching — rhyme, measure, and ordered verse help learners remember rules and lessons (historical practice: rules in verse). Also notes fitness for musical setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versifying is not equivalent to true poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not rhyming and versing that maketh poesy; one may be a poet without versing, and a versifier without poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating technical versification or mere rhyme with substantive poetic quality; watch for 'tinkling sound of rhyme' or confused verses that merely beget one another without ordering toward meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet does not lie by inventing (fiction vs affirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet never affirmeth; to lie is to affirm that to be true which is false ... the poet telleth not for true but what should or should not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging truthfulness, distinguish rhetorical/figurative or allegorical invention from historical assertion — fictional naming or personification is not dishonesty if not claimed as factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid condemning art for abuses (abuse ≠ essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though poesy may be abused ... the abuse shall not give reproach to the abused; contrariwise ... whatsoever being abused, doth most harm, being rightly used ... doth most good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use vs. abuse: identify whether objectionable effects come from misuse (reader/writer) rather than the art itself; weigh potential harms against pedagogical and moral benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should avoid promoting lustful or scurrilous content
rubrics_metrics.description: They say the comedies rather teach, than reprehend, amorous conceits ... that even to the heroical Cupid hath ambitiously climbed ... many leaves of the poets’ books [may contain] lust, vanity, scurrility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate decorum and moral tone: guard against wanton shows, scurrility, or lewdness that corrupt the fancy rather than edify; compare to painter leaving out worthy subjects for wanton shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate art, imitation, and exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: That Dædalus ... hath three wings to bear itself up into the air of due commendation; that is art, imitation, and exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess craft development: the poet should study rules/art, imitate good models, and practise diligently; genius alone insufficient without these three supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order matter and words deliberately (avoid 'quodlibet')
rubrics_metrics.description: There being two principal parts, matter to be expressed by words, and words to express the matter ... our matter is 'quodlibet' ... never marshalling it into any assured rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural planning: check for coherent arrangement of material and purposeful diction — avoid random accumulation of lines where one verse merely begets another without an intended order or endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe unity of place and time on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage should always represent but one place; and the uttermost time presupposed in it should be ... but one day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For drama, respect Aristotelian unities or stage plausibility: don't scatter action across many places/times that force constant explanatory entrances or strain credulity (example: Gorboduc's faults).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin the play at the principal point (not 'ab ovo')
rubrics_metrics.description: They must not begin 'ab ovo,' but they must come to the principal point of that one action which they will represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic economy: start at the decisive or climactic moment to maximize tragic/poetic focus (example: begin with discovery of Polydorus' body rather than the child's delivery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'nuntius' (narration) for off-stage or past events
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things may be told, which cannot be showed ... the ancients took by some 'Nuntius' to recount things done in former time, or other place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt storytelling to medium: report what cannot plausibly be represented on stage instead of attempting impossible scenic depictions (armies, distant lands, long durations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not improperly mix kings and clowns (maintain genre decorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: How all their plays be neither right tragedies nor right comedies, mingling kings and clowns ... thrust in the clown by head and shoulders to play a part in majestical matters, with neither decency nor discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve tonal consistency: avoid inserting low comic buffoonery into elevated tragic action unless it is artfully justified by genre precedent and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should provide delight, not mere laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Our comedians think there is no delight without laughter, which is very wrong; for though laughter may come with delight, yet cometh it not of delight ... the whole tract of a comedy should be full of delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comedic quality beyond jokes: measure whether the comedy delivers sustained delight, wit, and moral or social insight rather than crude mirth alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect stage constraints; don't attempt impossible representations
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot represent Peru or Calicut on stage without proper means; in action I cannot represent it without Pacolet’s horse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical staging: adapt plots so that what is shown is representable; rely on speech/reporting for distant or complex elements rather than contrived scenic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain civility and avoid scurrility in plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Their plays ... observe rules neither of honest civility nor skilful poetry ... we have nothing but scurrility, unworthy of any chaste ears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate language and manners: avoid indecent or base expressions that offend the audience's sense of propriety; uphold 'honest civility' in tone and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from exemplary predecessors; study classical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaucer ... the Earl of Surrey’s Lyrics ... The 'Shepherds’ Kalendar' ... but few printed that have poetical sinews in them ... if most of the verses be put in prose, one verse did but beget another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use models (Chaucer, Virgil, Theocritus, Seneca, Terence) to inform style and structure; study their ordering of material and avoidance of mere accumulative versifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek desert and craftsmanship; avoid unearned publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Base men with servile wits undertake it, who think it enough if they can be rewarded of the printer ... 'bastard poets' by publishing without proper merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authorial seriousness: prefer works showing merit, craft, and study over careless publications produced solely for printers' reward; encourage self-scrutiny before publishing.
